missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to recognise/draw simple diagrams to model the difference between solids, liquids and gases.
missing_spec_content.why: Every key point has "diagram": null. The lesson never describes or asks the student to draw particle diagrams for solids, liquids and gases.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Dimensions to be measured using appropriate apparatus such as a ruler, micrometer or Vernier callipers.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only names a ruler (keyPoints[2].content: "Measure its size with a ruler"). It never mentions a micrometer or Vernier callipers, or choosing apparatus to suit the size of the object.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to recall and apply this equation to changes where mass is conserved.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never says that mass is conserved during a change of state, so that a change in volume causes a change in density. It gives no example applying ρ = m/V to such a change.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to explain the differences in density between the different states of matter in terms of the arrangement of atoms or molecules.
missing_spec_content.why: This is only partly covered. Gases ("particles are very far apart") and solids ("packed more tightly") are described. The general arrangement of particles in a liquid (close together but irregular and able to move) is never stated, except as "jumbled" in the water/ice exception.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The particle model can be used to explain - the different states of matter
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson uses the particle model only for density. It does not use it to explain the states themselves, for example particle arrangement and movement in solids, liquids and gases.

above_gcse.text: In ice, water molecules form a regular, open hexagonal lattice. Forces of attraction between the molecules hold it together. This open structure takes up MORE space than the jumbled arrangement in liquid water.
above_gcse.why: The specification does not require the anomalous density of ice or its hexagonal crystal structure. The topic is also reinforced in writeBullets, keyTerms ("Hexagonal lattice"), revisionCardBullets and checkpoint 3, so it may displace the core idea that solids are generally densest.
Extra detail that this specification section does not require.

above_gcse.text: Floating and sinking: compare the object with the fluid it is in. An object floats if it is less dense than the fluid.
above_gcse.why: Floating and sinking is not part of 4.3.1.1. It is presented with examFlag and appears in checkpoints, revision cards and examTips as if this section examines it.

above_gcse.text: Liquid aluminium: ~2375 kg/m³ (slightly less dense, as particles are slightly further apart)
above_gcse.why: Specific data for molten metals is beyond what the specification requires.

above_gcse.text:
Lakes freeze from the top down. Ice forms at the surface and insulates the water below
- Water life can survive under ice in winter
above_gcse.why: This application of the ice anomaly is not required by the specification.

factual_errors.text: Volume of displaced water = volume of the irregular object (Archimedes' principle)
factual_errors.correction: Archimedes' principle states that the upthrust on an object equals the weight of fluid it displaces. The fact that a fully submerged object displaces its own volume of liquid is simply displacement, not Archimedes' principle.

factual_errors.text: It explains why the air gets thinner the higher you go.
factual_errors.correction: Air getting thinner means its density decreases with height. The cause is that there is less air above pressing down, so pressure is lower. Density describes the effect; it does not explain it.

checkpoint_mismatch.key_point: keyPoints[1] "Calculating density — worked examples" (rearrangements m = ρV, V = m/ρ and the unit conversion 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³)
checkpoint_mismatch.why: The checkpoint is a direct ρ = m/V calculation in g/cm³, essentially the same as checkpoint 0. It tests neither rearranging the equation nor converting between g/cm³ and kg/m³, which are the main content of this key point.
